Diversifying your Alphas is indeed key to reducing both self-correlation and production correlation. By exploring unique data sources, timeframes, or methodologies, you can create Alphas that complement each other while maintaining distinct signals. Avoid overfitting your models to pass submission tests, as this can harm real-world performance. Instead, focus on robust, generalizable signals that perform consistently across different scenarios. Regularly validate your Alphas on out-of-sample data to ensure they aren’t overly tailored to specific conditions. Collaboration and sharing insights, as suggested, help everyone improve—diverse perspectives lead to better ideas and stronger Alphas. Some ways:

- Use new operators

- Work on unexplored datasets, especially ones with high "Value score". They might even gain you weight quicker.

- Submit alphas in less explored regions like - EU,AMR,GLB; this will likely improve your combined alpha performance; and you can create alphas similar to USA in these regions.

- Read research papers, try to find ways in which researchers measure various qualities of a firm, and ways in which they find inefficiencies in price discovery

Great points!

To add, here are some strategies that have worked for me:

Vary Data Sources: Use alphas based on different types of data (fundamental, technical, sentiment, alternative) to reduce overlap.

Experiment with Regions and Asset Classes: Submitting alphas across diverse regions or asset classes can help lower production correlation.

Test Across Market Conditions: Ensure alphas perform robustly in different regimes (e.g., bull, bear, sideway) to avoid overfitting.

Use Neutralization: Apply neutralization at the sector or market level to focus on unique stock-level signals.

It’s all about creativity and testing. Let’s keep building better alphas together! 😊
